big: The easiest mistake in picking funds is buying many. Twelve funds feel like a spread. Often they are the same stocks, held twelve times.

lines: My colleague gave me 12 good funds. Can I buy all of them?
Let us count how many different stocks she would really own.

alt: Bars showing the number of different stocks rising slowly as funds are added
caps: One fund holds about 40 different stocks.
A second adds only 18 new ones, because most of its stocks are already in the first.
By twelve funds, she owns 78 different stocks. Most of the money is in the same companies.

h: Many funds, or a few with jobs
alt: Twelve similar slices against three slices with different jobs
caps: Twelve funds from one category do one job twelve times.
Three funds with different jobs spread the risk, and are easier to watch.

q: A friend suggests twelve equity funds. What is the best response?
opts: Buy all twelve, since more funds always means more spread
Check the overlap, then pick a few that do different jobs
Buy the six with the highest returns of the last year
Buy one fund from each fund house, to keep it fair
why: More names rarely mean more spread. If the funds hold the same stocks, a fall hits all of them together.
Overlap shows how many stocks repeat. A few funds with different jobs add real spread and are simple to follow.
Last year's winners are often at their peak. A one-year return says little about the next decade.
Fund houses are not a measure of spread. Two funds from different houses can hold the same stocks.

q: What is the better way to compare two equity funds in the same category?
opts: Their return in the last calendar year, taken by itself
Whichever fund house spends more on its advertising
Whichever one has the more famous fund manager running it
Rolling returns over several periods, plus downside and cost
why: A single year can be a lucky one. It hides how the fund behaved across good and bad markets.
Advertising spend has no link to how a fund performs. It is paid from fees at some level.
A famous name tells you little. Check the manager's tenure and how the fund held up in bad years.
Rolling periods show consistency, the bad-year numbers show risk, and cost shows what is kept. Together they paint a fair picture.

q: In the made-up holdings, twelve funds owned only 78 different stocks. What does this suggest?
opts: Same-category funds hold many of the same stocks, so extras add little
Every fund that is added brings an almost entirely new set of stocks
Twelve is the ideal number of funds for an investor of any kind
Overlap of holdings is a problem seen only in debt mutual funds
why: The first few funds add most of the spread. After that, more funds repeat the same companies and cost time.
The bars show the opposite. The count of new stocks grows slowly because most are already owned.
No ideal number fits everyone. The right number depends on the jobs the funds do, not a count.
Equity funds overlap often, especially in the same category where managers look at the same large companies.

q: Why can a very large size hurt a mid or small cap fund?
opts: A larger fund must pay a higher rate of tax on the gains it makes
Large funds are not allowed to hold any small company stocks at all
Large positions in thinly traded stocks move the price as they trade
The fund house is forced to close down any scheme once it gets big
why: Tax does not rise with fund size. The concern is about trading, not about a larger tax bill.
Large funds are allowed to hold small stocks. The difficulty is in trading them in volume.
Mid and small stocks trade in smaller volumes. A big fund buying or selling can push the price, which raises its costs.
A fund is not closed for being large. Some funds limit new money so that the strategy still works.

pts: Start with the goal and horizon, then the category, then compare funds.
Compare over rolling periods. Look at consistency, bad years, concentration and cost.
Hold a few funds that do different jobs. Overlap adds paperwork, not spread.
